svg.aria-label: Diagram: how a KMS grant differs from a key policy statement, and what each difference costs. A grant is described by AWS as a policy instrument allowing AWS principals or service principals to use KMS keys in cryptographic operations, and grants are considered alongside key policies and IAM policies when authorizing access. Five structural differences are set out. First, a grant is a resource with a quota: each customer managed key can have up to fifty thousand grants including those created by AWS services integrated with KMS, the quota is adjustable, and it does not apply to AWS managed or AWS owned keys. That quota is a concurrency limit rather than a configuration limit, because AWS states you cannot perform more than fifty thousand grant-authorized operations using the same key at the same time, and after reaching it new grants can only be created when an active grant is retired or revoked; AWS's worked example is that EBS creates a grant for each volume attachment, so if every volume uses the same key you cannot attach more than fifty thousand volumes at once. Second, a grant has no modify operation: the enumerated grant operations are the cryptographic operations plus CreateGrant, DescribeKey, GetPublicKey and RetireGrant, so changing a grant means deleting it and creating another. Third, a grant is eventually consistent in both directions: creating, retiring or revoking may take up to about five minutes to propagate, a grant token returned only by CreateGrant lets the new permissions be used immediately, and on deletion the grantee principal might still be able to use the permissions for a brief period until the grant is fully deleted. A grant token can retire a grant but cannot revoke one, and CreateGrant is the only source of a token: it cannot be read from ListGrants or from CloudTrail. Fourth, the grant decides who may delete it: revoking is a normal key-policy and IAM-policy permission held by key administrators, while retiring is determined by the retiring principal or retiring service principal named in the grant, by the grantee if the grant includes the RetireGrant operation, or by the account where the grant was created. AWS states the kms RetireGrant permission has limited utility, that principals named in the grant can retire without it, that the permission alone does not allow retiring, and that it is not effective in a key policy or a resource control policy, leaving only its use as a Deny in an IAM policy. Fifth, kms CreateGrant is a privilege escalation primitive: AWS compares it to kms PutKeyPolicy and states that principals who get the permission from a policy can create grants for any grant operation and are not required to hold the permission they are granting, though principals who get CreateGrant from a grant can only delegate what they themselves were granted, so a grant chain cannot widen. A panel records the retry trap: without the Name parameter every CreateGrant call produces a new grant with a unique grant identifier even when all parameters are identical, so a retry loop creates duplicates against the fifty thousand ceiling, while supplying Name makes the call idempotent and returns the original grant identifier, though the grant token is still unique per request. A closing panel records the grant constraints: EncryptionContextEquals and EncryptionContextSubset, limited to eight encryption context pairs and three hundred and eighty four characters per constraint value and unsupported on asymmetric and HMAC keys, and SourceArn which works on all key types; both carve out RetireGrant, to which the constraints do not apply, and AWS warns that constraint and name fields may appear in plaintext in CloudTrail logs.
svg.title: A grant is not a policy statement: five differences, five failures
svg.text: “Policy instrument” files it with key policies and IAM policies. Almost nothing transfers.
A statement is edited in place and effective at once. A grant is replaced, counted, and slow in both directions.
1 · It is a resource, and the ceiling is a concurrency limit in disguise
50,000 grants per customer managed key — “including the grants created by AWS services”. Adjustable.
“you cannot perform more than 50,000 grant-authorized operations that use the same KMS key at the same time”
AWS’s example: EBS creates a grant per volume attachment → one key for every volume means
you “cannot attach more than 50,000 volumes at one time”. You create none of those grants.
2 · There is no modify operation
grant operations = the cryptographic ones, plus
CreateGrant · DescribeKey · GetPublicKey · RetireGrant
Tightening a constraint = create the new one,
delete the old. Order decides what you risk.
3 · Eventually consistent both ways
create → “usually less than five minutes”; fix with a
grant token, returned only by CreateGrant
delete → grantee “might still be able to use its
permissions for a brief period”. No token fix: a
token can retire a grant, never revoke one.
4 · The grant decides who can delete it — and the obvious permission barely works
Revoke — normal: kms:RevokeGrant via key policy / IAM, “included in the standard permissions given to key administrators”.
Retire — “The grant determines who can retire it”: the RetiringPrincipal named inside, the grantee if the grant
includes RetireGrant, or the account where it was created.
kms:RetireGrant “has limited utility” · principals in the grant can retire “without” it · it “alone does not allow” retiring
· “not effective in a key policy or resource control policy” → its one use is a Deny in an IAM policy.
5 · kms:CreateGrant hands out permissions the holder does not have
“Permission to create grants has security implications, much like allowing the kms:PutKeyPolicy permission”
“These principals are not required to have the permission that they are granting on the key.”
But from a grant: “can only delegate the permissions that they were granted, even if they have other
permissions from a policy” → a grant chain cannot widen. Delegate through a grant, not the key policy.
The retry trap meets the ceiling
No Name → “all CreateGrant requests result in a
new grant with a unique GrantId even if all the
supplied parameters are identical”.
A retry loop fills slots and succeeds every time.
Constraints, and the hole in both
EncryptionContext Equals / Subset — 8 pairs max,
384 chars per value, symmetric keys only
SourceArn — all key types
Neither applies to RetireGrant. Again.
And the grant document is published: on Constraints and Name — “may be displayed in plaintext in CloudTrail logs and other output.”
A grantee cannot be a service principal, an IAM group or an organization; each grant covers exactly one key. Counts grow multiplicatively.
Supply Name on every call. Set RetiringPrincipal at creation, because no policy can add it later. Then count your grants.
They are a resource, and the thing about resources is that you can run out.
